title: When the lesion is everywhere: coma and diffuse disease
description: How to localize a child who cannot cooperate, covering the two places where consciousness lives, the coma examination as a way of finding the level, the choice between metabolic and structural coma, herniation, and diffuse disease.
why: Some findings refuse to point to a single level, and recognizing that pattern is itself a localization.
objectives: Explain why depressed consciousness localizes to the brainstem tegmentum or to both hemispheres, and what a one-sided lesion must do to cause coma.
Use breathing, pupils, eye movements and motor responses to place a coma at one level, or to recognize that the signs do not agree.
Separate metabolic and toxic coma from structural coma at the bedside, and act on the difference.
Recognize uncal herniation from the pupil, and explain why the hemiparesis may sit on the wrong side.
Treat diffuse and multifocal disease in a child as an address in its own right, and carry it into a differential.

sections.title: Consciousness lives in two places
sections.content:
Every other module in this curriculum asks the patient to do something, whether that means squeezing your fingers, following a target, walking across the room or reporting a pinprick. A child in coma can do none of it, which is exactly why coma belongs in a course on localization. When the patient cannot cooperate, the anatomy has to speak through reflexes, and the first reflex worth reading is consciousness itself.

**Two structures, working together**

Wakefulness depends on an interaction between the **ascending reticular activating system** in the brainstem and the **cerebral hemispheres** (Brazis 2011, p. 604). In people the activating system lies in the paramedian tegmentum of the pons and midbrain, which leaves coma with only two honest addresses, a lesion in that small tegmental core or dysfunction of **both** hemispheres at once.

That has real force at the bedside, because a lesion confined to **one hemisphere** does not, on its own, abolish consciousness. A child with a large one-sided stroke or tumor may be aphasic, hemiplegic and miserable, and still be awake. If that child becomes unresponsive, something has changed. The lesion may have grown or swollen enough to press on the brainstem, a second process may have appeared on the other side, or the child may be seizing without convulsing. Unresponsiveness in a child with a one-sided lesion is therefore a **new localizing sign**, and usually an emergency.

**Say what you saw**

Words such as lethargic, obtunded and stuporous feel precise, yet they carry much less information than they seem to. Brazis argues instead for describing responsiveness in plain words, saying what the child did, to which stimulus, and how quickly the response faded (Brazis 2011, p. 603). A note that reads "Opened her eyes to her name, looked at her mother, then drifted off without speaking" can be compared at the next examination by someone else, which is more than "lethargic" allows. The stimuli suited to a child are different, such as a parent's voice, a favorite toy or a feed, but the principle is the same, and what goes in the notes should be the behavior you watched rather than the label you would give it.

The rest of this module applies the same discipline to the brainstem reflexes, which keep working when the child cannot, and to the diffuse diseases that make "everywhere" a genuine answer instead of a failure to localize.
keyPoints: Consciousness needs the brainstem reticular activating system (paramedian tegmentum of the pons and midbrain) and both hemispheres (Brazis 2011, p. 604).
A lesion confined to one hemisphere does not cause coma on its own, so coma in that setting suggests brainstem compression, a second lesion or non-convulsive seizures.
Describe responsiveness in plain words, naming the stimulus and the response, rather than with labels such as lethargic or stuporous (Brazis 2011, p. 603).
When the child cannot cooperate, the brainstem reflexes become the examination.

question.question: A 9-year-old with a known left frontal tumor has been awake and talking with a right hemiparesis. Overnight she becomes hard to rouse, opening her eyes only to a firm sternal rub and not speaking. What does the change in consciousness tell you?
options: Nothing new about localization, since the tumor is in the left hemisphere and hemispheric lesions cause sleepiness
A new process is involving the brainstem or the other hemisphere, such as swelling with herniation or non-convulsive seizures, and it needs urgent assessment
The tumor has spread along the corticospinal tract, which explains both the weakness and the drowsiness
She is post-ictal after an unwitnessed seizure, so observation without imaging is appropriate
question.explanation: Consciousness depends on the brainstem reticular activating system and both hemispheres working together, so a lesion confined to one hemisphere does not abolish it. When a child with a one-sided tumor becomes unresponsive, something new has happened, whether swelling that compresses the brainstem, a second lesion, or seizures without convulsions. Treating the drowsiness as an expected feature of a hemispheric tumor misses that it is a new localizing sign. Spread along the corticospinal tract would worsen the weakness but could not explain coma. A post-ictal state is possible, but you reach that conclusion only after excluding herniation and ongoing seizures, so it is no reason to skip imaging and an EEG.

sections.title: The coma exam as a level-finder
sections.content:
Once the patient's cooperation has been taken away, the coma examination is what remains of localization. Four things still work without any effort from the child, the **pattern of breathing**, the **pupils**, the **eye movements** and the **motor response to pain**, and each of them has a level written into it (Pearl 2014, pp. 94-97). Use the figure above to set each one and watch whether they agree.

**Breathing.** Breathing that waxes and wanes with pauses between (Cheyne-Stokes) points to both hemispheres or the diencephalon. Sustained, fast, deep breathing points to the low midbrain or upper pons, long pauses at full inspiration (apneustic breathing) point to the pons, and chaotic, irregular breathing points to the medulla, where the respiratory rhythm is generated (Pearl 2014, pp. 94-95).

**Pupils.** Small pupils that still react fit diencephalic or metabolic depression (Brazis 2011, p. 608). A midbrain lesion interrupts the light reflex, so the pupils lose their reactivity, while a pontine lesion cuts the descending sympathetic fibers and leaves the pupils pinpoint (Pearl 2014, p. 95).

**Eye movements.** When the head of a comatose child with an intact brainstem is turned, the eyes float to the opposite side, like an expensive doll's eyes (Pearl 2014, p. 96). Cold water in the ear is a stronger stimulus, and it should turn the eyes toward the ice. If it does, the brainstem from the upper medulla to the midbrain is working. In coma there is no fast phase, because nystagmus needs the cortex.

**Motor response.** Flexion of the arms with extended legs places the lesion between the cortex and the upper midbrain, extension of all four limbs places it between the midbrain and the pontomedullary junction, and flaccidity places it below that (Pearl 2014, p. 97).

**Putting it together.** If breathing, pupils, eyes and posture all point to the same level, a single structural lesion there fits. If they **disagree**, the process is probably multifocal, and multifocal coma is most often metabolic. If they **move downward** over hours, think of herniation (Pearl 2014, p. 97). Children are scored with modified versions of the adult coma scales (Pearl 2014, p. 147), but the logic of finding the level is the same at every age.
keyPoints: Breathing, pupils, eye movements and motor responses each point to a level, and all four keep working when the child cannot cooperate (Pearl 2014, pp. 94-97).
Pinpoint pupils with apneustic breathing and absent horizontal eye movements point to the pons, while small reactive pupils fit diencephalic or metabolic depression (Brazis 2011, p. 608).
Eyes that turn toward cold water in the ear show that the brainstem from medulla to midbrain is working.
Signs that agree suggest one structural lesion, signs that disagree suggest multifocal and usually metabolic disease, and signs that move downward suggest herniation (Pearl 2014, p. 97).

question.question: A 12-year-old is found unresponsive. She has long pauses at the top of each breath, pinpoint pupils, no horizontal eye movement when the head is turned, and extends all four limbs to pain. Where is the lesion, and what kind of process does the pattern suggest?
options: Both hemispheres, from a metabolic cause, because she is in coma
The medulla, because breathing is abnormal
The pons, from a single structural lesion, because every sign points to the same level
The midbrain, because extensor posturing always means a midbrain lesion
question.explanation: Apneustic breathing, pinpoint pupils, absent horizontal doll's-eye movements and extensor posturing all point to the pons, and when every sign agrees on one level a single structural lesion there is the best fit. In a child that means looking urgently for hemorrhage, a vascular event or a pontine tumor. Hemispheric or metabolic coma gives small reactive pupils and intact doll's eyes, which is not what she shows. Medullary breathing is chaotic rather than apneustic. Extensor posturing marks the whole span from the midbrain to the pontomedullary junction, so it is consistent with a pontine lesion and cannot by itself pin the lesion to the midbrain.

sections.title: Metabolic or structural?
sections.content:
At the bedside of a comatose child, the most useful early decision concerns the **kind** of problem more than its level. Either a structural lesion is pressing on the brain, or the brain is being poisoned or starved, and the distinction matters because the two are managed differently and one of them can often be corrected within minutes.

**The clue that the books keep returning to**

In metabolic coma the **pupils may still react when the eye movements are gone** (Brazis 2011, p. 610). The pupillary light reflex is one of the most resistant reflexes in the brainstem, so a drug or a metabolic derangement can silence the eye movements while the small pupils still constrict to light. A structural lesion that destroys horizontal eye movements, by contrast, usually takes the pupils with it, because the pathways sit close together. Reactive pupils with absent eye movements therefore point away from a structural brainstem lesion and toward the blood.

**Drugs can do anything**

Pearl's warning that drugs can do anything is worth memorizing (Pearl 2014, p. 96). Anticholinergics and stimulants dilate the pupils, while barbiturates, benzodiazepines and other sedatives constrict them, and most sedative overdoses do not abolish the light reflex (Brazis 2011, p. 608). A toddler who has found a grandparent's tablets can produce a coma examination that mimics almost any level.

**What points to structure**

Asymmetry favors a structural diagnosis, whether it shows as one pupil larger than the other, a gaze deviation, a hemiparesis or posturing on one side, and so does a pattern that **descends** over hours. Symmetry, fluctuation and signs that refuse to agree on a level point the other way (Pearl 2014, p. 97).

**In a child**

The metabolic list in children is long and urgent. It includes low glucose, ingestion, high ammonia, diabetic ketoacidosis, infection and non-convulsive seizures, and the last of these is a reason to involve the [EEG curriculum](/eeg) early. However long the list, the practical rule stays simple. Check the glucose at once, look for a chemical cause while you examine, and image urgently whenever the examination is asymmetric or worsening.
keyPoints: Reactive pupils with absent eye movements are the classic sign of metabolic or toxic coma (Brazis 2011, p. 610).
Drugs can do anything to the pupils, with anticholinergics and stimulants dilating them and sedatives constricting them (Pearl 2014, p. 96).
Asymmetry and a descending pattern point to a structural lesion, while symmetry and signs that disagree point to metabolic disease.
In every comatose child, check the glucose immediately and look for a chemical cause while the examination proceeds.

question.question: A 2-year-old is brought in very drowsy after playing unsupervised at a relative's house. Her pupils are small and react briskly to light, she has no horizontal eye movement on head turning, and her limbs are symmetrically floppy. What is the most appropriate interpretation and first step?
options: A pontine hemorrhage, because horizontal eye movements are absent; arrange neurosurgical review before anything else
Probably toxic or metabolic, because the pupils react despite absent eye movements; check the glucose at once and start a toxic and metabolic search, imaging if anything becomes asymmetric
Brain death must be considered, because the doll's-eye response is absent
A functional unresponsiveness, because the examination is symmetric
question.explanation: Reactive pupils despite absent eye movements are the dissociation that points to metabolic or toxic coma, and in a toddler who had an unsupervised opportunity an ingestion heads the list. The first steps are the ones that can be corrected quickly, starting with the glucose and then a toxic and metabolic screen, with imaging if the examination becomes asymmetric or worsens. A pontine hemorrhage usually takes the pupils along with the eye movements and leaves them pinpoint and poorly reactive. Brain death requires absent brainstem reflexes, including the pupillary reflex, which here is working. A symmetric examination is typical of metabolic coma and offers no evidence of a functional disorder.

sections.title: Herniation: when the lesion moves
sections.content:
A mass inside a closed skull does not stay where it started. It pushes brain from one compartment into another, and the signs then belong to the place being squeezed rather than to the place where the trouble began, so the localization itself moves while you watch.

**Uncal herniation and the pupil**

An expanding mass in one temporal lobe can push the uncus over the edge of the tentorium and onto the third nerve and the midbrain (Pearl 2014, pp. 37, 93). The pupil-constricting fibers run on the outside of the third nerve, so external pressure dilates the pupil early, on the **same side** as the mass, and a progressive third-nerve palsy and falling consciousness follow.

The hemiparesis is a less reliable guide. In principle the mass should weaken the opposite side, through the corticospinal tract on its own side, but the shifting midbrain can be pressed against the opposite edge of the tentorium, notching the other cerebral peduncle (Kernohan's notch) and weakening the limbs on the **same side** as the mass. Pearl's blunt conclusion is that in uncal herniation the dilated pupil reliably tells the side of the lesion, and the hemiparesis may not (Pearl 2014, p. 37).

**The other directions**

The cingulate gyrus can slide under the falx and compress the territory of the anterior cerebral artery, weakening the opposite leg. Swelling of both hemispheres pushes the diencephalon straight down, producing progressive dysfunction of both sides of the brainstem from the top. Cerebellar tonsils pushed through the foramen magnum compress the medulla, and then breathing and circulation can fail abruptly (Pearl 2014, pp. 92-93). A widening pulse pressure with a slowing pulse and changing breathing is the body's late warning that the pressure has risen (Pearl 2014, p. 94).

**Watching the level fall**

The coma signs from section 2 are the best monitor. When breathing changes from Cheyne-Stokes to sustained hyperventilation, the pupils move from small and reactive to fixed, and posturing moves from flexion to extension, a level that descends over hours like this should be treated as herniation unless something else clearly explains it (Pearl 2014, p. 97). To see it happen, return to the coma figure in section 2 and press **Watch a herniation descend**, and breathing, pupils, eyes and posture will change stage by stage until the level stops being a place and becomes a trajectory. Posterior fossa tumors in children make the downward, tonsillar direction a particular concern, and a lumbar puncture in a child with signs of raised pressure and a mass can precipitate it.
keyPoints: In uncal herniation the pupil on the side of the mass dilates first, because the pupillary fibers run on the outside of the third nerve (Pearl 2014, pp. 36-37).
The hemiparesis can be on the same side as the mass (Kernohan's notch), so the pupil is the more reliable guide to the side (Pearl 2014, p. 37).
Tonsillar herniation compresses the medulla and can stop breathing and circulation abruptly (Pearl 2014, p. 93).
A level that descends over hours on serial coma examinations should be treated as herniation unless something else clearly explains it (Pearl 2014, p. 97).

question.question: A 14-year-old is brought in after a fall from a bicycle. He was talking, then became drowsy. His right pupil is dilated and sluggish, and his RIGHT arm and leg are weaker than the left. On which side is the expanding lesion most likely to be?
options: Left, because the hemiparesis is on the right and the corticospinal tract crosses
It cannot be told, because the signs conflict
Both sides equally, so bilateral surgery should be planned
Right, because the dilated pupil reliably marks the side of uncal herniation, and the same-side weakness can come from the opposite peduncle being notched on the tentorium
question.explanation: In uncal herniation the pupil-constricting fibers on the outside of the third nerve are compressed first, so the dilated pupil is on the side of the mass. The weakness can be on the same side when the shifted midbrain presses the opposite cerebral peduncle against the tentorium, which is Kernohan's notch, and that is why the pupil is the more reliable sign. Reading the right hemiparesis in the usual crossed way would send you to the wrong side. The signs seem to conflict only if you trust the weakness over the pupil, and nothing in the story suggests two lesions that would call for operating on both sides.

sections.title: False localizing signs
sections.content:
Most of this module has been about signs that agree with one another. The signs in this section mislead, or, to be fairer to them, answer a question you did not ask. A **false localizing sign** is produced by a process at a distance, through pressure, shift or a chemical, rather than by damage at the address the sign usually names.

**The messenger and the address**

[[m07-brainstem|Module 7]] met the child with morning headaches, vomiting and double vision on looking to one side. The sixth nerve's long course makes it an early casualty of raised intracranial pressure, whether from tumors above or below the tentorium, hydrocephalus or pseudotumor cerebri (Pearl 2014, pp. 43, 48; Brazis 2011, p. 202). Brazis names sixth-nerve palsy and papilledema as the commonest false localizing signs, and he warns that a supratentorial process, especially a midline one causing hydrocephalus, can raise the pressure without focal signs and leave cranial nerve palsies that look like a posterior fossa lesion (Brazis 2011, p. 622). Posterior fossa tumors are common in children (Pearl 2014, p. 63), so the posterior fossa is a fair suspect, but all the sixth nerve has told you is that the pressure is up.

**The rest of the family**

- **The wrong-sided hemiparesis** of Kernohan's notch, already met in the herniation section (Brazis 2011, p. 616).
- **A sensory level that is too low**, when compression high in the cervical cord gives a sensory level on the trunk together with clumsy, wasted hands (Brazis 2011, p. 115).
- **Nystagmus from drugs**, since anticonvulsants can produce a central-looking nystagmus with no lesion in the brainstem (Pearl 2014, p. 121).
- **Anomia**, because word-finding failure is relatively nonlocalizing (Pearl 2014, p. 20; [[m09-hemispheres|Module 9]]).

**A sign that does localize**

Vertical gaze behaves differently, because a tumor pressing on the posterior commissure, such as a pineal tumor, disturbs it directly and can hold the eyes tonically downward in what is called Parinaud syndrome (Pearl 2014, p. 40). In a child with raised pressure, then, failure of upgaze gives you an address, while a sixth-nerve palsy is only a messenger.

> **Bedside trick.** When the eyes rest deviated to one side, turn the head passively. The doll's-eye movement overcomes the gaze preference of a cortical lesion, because the brainstem gaze center still works, but it cannot overcome the gaze palsy of a pontine lesion, where that center is gone (Pearl 2014, p. 45). Since the eyes look toward a cortical lesion and away from a pontine one (Pearl 2014, p. 43), this single maneuver settles both the level and the side.

**When a sign travels alone**

A sign that turns up without its usual companions deserves suspicion. Ask what company it would keep at a true address, and if that company is missing, read the sign as a report on pressure, shift or chemistry, and image the whole head rather than the spot it seems to name.
keyPoints: A false localizing sign is produced at a distance, by pressure, shift or a chemical, rather than by damage at the address it usually names.
Sixth-nerve palsy and papilledema are the commonest false localizing signs, and a supratentorial or midline process can imitate a posterior fossa lesion (Brazis 2011, p. 622).

Kernohan's notch, a sensory level from high cervical compression, drug-induced nystagmus and anomia all point to the wrong place or to nowhere in particular (Brazis 2011, pp. 115, 616; Pearl 2014, pp. 20, 121).
Failure of vertical gaze from pressure on the posterior commissure does localize, to the pineal region (Pearl 2014, p. 40).
Passive head turning overcomes a cortical gaze preference but not a pontine gaze palsy (Pearl 2014, p. 45).

question.question: An 8-year-old has had three weeks of morning headaches and vomiting. Both optic discs are swollen and neither eye abducts fully. There is no facial weakness, no gaze palsy, no ataxia and no long-tract sign. A colleague requests an MRI limited to the pons and posterior fossa. What do you advise?
options: Agree, because posterior fossa tumors are common in children and the sixth nerves arise from the pons
Do a lumbar puncture first to measure the opening pressure, then decide on imaging
Image the orbits to look for disease of the lateral rectus muscles
Image the whole brain urgently, because bilateral sixth-nerve palsies with papilledema report raised pressure, which a supratentorial or midline process can cause as readily as a posterior fossa one
question.explanation: Sixth-nerve palsy and papilledema are the commonest false localizing signs, because the long sixth nerve suffers from raised pressure wherever it comes from, and a supratentorial or midline lesion causing hydrocephalus can imitate a posterior fossa one (Brazis 2011, p. 622; Pearl 2014, p. 43). The posterior fossa is a fair suspect in a child (Pearl 2014, p. 63), which is what makes the limited scan tempting, but the palsies do not place the lesion there, and a limited study could miss the cause. A lumbar puncture before imaging in a child with raised pressure risks herniation. Swollen discs point to a problem inside the skull, so imaging the orbits would look in the wrong place.

sections.title: Diffuse and multifocal disease in children
sections.content:
Localization trains you to look for the single point where the findings meet, and sometimes there is no such point. The honest answer is then "everywhere", which is a result in its own right and narrows the differential as sharply as any address on the [[m01-where-before-what|level ladder]].

**Discrete lesions and system disease**

Brazis draws the distinction by noting that much of localization was learned from discrete lesions such as infarcts, tumors, abscesses and plaques, while other diseases attack whole arrays of neurons that share a job (Brazis 2011, p. 4). The first kind gives signs that meet at one point, and the second gives signs that respect a system, a tract or a cell type instead of a place.

**Three ways a child's brain is everywhere**

- **Diffuse:** an encephalopathy from a toxin, an infection, a metabolic derangement or prolonged seizures, in which consciousness falls, the signs are symmetric, and the coma examination refuses to settle on a level.
- **Multifocal:** several discrete lesions at once. Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis after an infection is the classic pediatric example, a sleepy child with signs from the hemispheres, the brainstem and the cord that no single lesion can explain.
- **System:** a genetic or metabolic disease that takes one kind of tissue throughout the nervous system, such as the white matter in a leukodystrophy or the gray matter in a neuronal storage disease.

**Regression: localization in time**

In a child, "everywhere" often shows itself as a loss rather than a coma, with skills that were once present and are now gone. Regression localizes the process in time as clearly as a sensory level localizes it in space, because it says that the disease is active now. It also moves the differential toward the neurodegenerative, genetic and metabolic causes, the epileptic encephalopathies and acquired encephalitis that the next module sets out in its grid.

Whatever the pattern, the decision that follows is the same. Name the pattern as diffuse, multifocal or system, and then let the tempo of the illness choose among the causes, using the grid that [[m11-where-to-what|Module 11]] builds.
keyPoints: "Everywhere" is itself a localization, because diffuse, multifocal and system patterns each narrow the differential.
Discrete lesions give signs that meet at a point, whereas system diseases give signs that respect a tract or cell type throughout the nervous system (Brazis 2011, p. 4).
Signs from several levels at once in a sleepy child after an infection suggest a multifocal process such as acute disseminated encephalomyelitis.
Regression, the loss of skills already acquired, localizes a process in time and points toward neurodegenerative, genetic and metabolic causes and epileptic encephalopathy.

question.question: A 6-year-old became sleepy and irritable ten days after a viral illness. She now has a mild left hemiparesis, unsteady arms, double vision and difficulty passing urine. No single lesion explains all of this. What is the most useful way to frame her localization?
options: Multifocal central nervous system disease, which points toward an acute inflammatory demyelinating process and calls for imaging of the brain and the whole spine
Brainstem, because double vision is present, so imaging of the posterior fossa alone is enough
Non-localizing, so localization adds nothing and broad testing should replace it
Peripheral nerve, because the bladder is involved
question.explanation: Signs from a hemisphere (the hemiparesis), from the brainstem or cerebellar connections (the double vision and unsteadiness) and from the cord (the bladder) cannot come from one lesion. That makes the localization multifocal, which after an infection points toward acute disseminated encephalomyelitis and tells you to image the brain and the whole spine. Settling on the brainstem alone ignores the bladder and the hemiparesis, and imaging only the posterior fossa could miss the cord. Calling the picture non-localizing throws away information, since multifocal is itself an answer that narrows the field. A peripheral nerve problem cannot explain drowsiness or double vision with a hemiparesis.

quiz.question: A 4-year-old is comatose after a cardiac arrest. Breathing is Cheyne-Stokes, the pupils are small and reactive, the eyes move fully with head turning, and the arms flex to pain. A colleague asks where the lesion is. What is the best answer?
options: The medulla, because breathing is irregular
Both hemispheres or the diencephalon, with the brainstem working, because every sign points to that level
The pons, because the pupils are small
The midbrain, because there is posturing
quiz.explanation: Cheyne-Stokes breathing, small reactive pupils, intact doll's-eye movements and flexor posturing all point to the level above the midbrain, meaning both hemispheres or the diencephalon with a working brainstem, which fits a diffuse hypoxic insult. Medullary breathing is chaotic rather than waxing and waning. Pontine pupils are pinpoint, and pontine lesions abolish the horizontal doll's-eye movements that are present here. Flexor posturing places the lesion between the cortex and the upper midbrain, so it agrees with the hemispheric level and does not single out the midbrain.

quiz.question: An adolescent is comatose. His pupils react to light, but cold water in either ear produces no eye movement at all, and his limbs are symmetrically flaccid. Breathing is shallow but regular. What does this combination suggest?
options: A structural lesion of the whole brainstem, so the outlook is hopeless
Brain death, because there is no caloric response
A toxic or metabolic cause such as a sedative overdose, because the pupils still react when the eye movements are gone
Locked-in syndrome, because he is not moving
quiz.explanation: The pupillary light reflex is among the most resistant reflexes of the brainstem, and in metabolic coma the pupils may still react when eye movements cannot be elicited. Reactive pupils with absent calorics therefore point toward a drug or metabolic cause, which may be fully reversible. A structural lesion destroying the brainstem would usually take the pupils too, so calling the outlook hopeless is both wrong and dangerous. Brain death requires absent pupillary reflexes, and his are present. A locked-in patient is awake, with preserved vertical eye or eyelid movements, whereas this boy is comatose with absent calorics.

quiz.question: A child with a left temporal abscess becomes drowsy. Over two hours his breathing changes from waxing and waning to fast and deep, the left pupil enlarges and stops reacting, and his flexor posturing becomes extensor. What is happening?
options: Transtentorial herniation, because the level of dysfunction is descending through the brainstem
Recovery, because his breathing is now regular
A new seizure focus in the right hemisphere
A medullary stroke, because breathing has changed
quiz.explanation: Each sign has moved down a level, with breathing shifting from the hemispheric pattern to the midbrain pattern, the pupil from reactive to fixed and posture from flexion to extension. A level that descends over hours should be treated as herniation, and a dilating pupil on the side of the abscess fits uncal herniation, so this is an emergency. Regular deep breathing in this setting reflects midbrain involvement and is no sign of recovery. A seizure would not produce a fixed dilated pupil with descending signs, and a medullary stroke does not explain a sequence that begins in the hemispheres.

quiz.question: Why does a lesion confined to one cerebral hemisphere not usually cause coma on its own?
options: Because the cortex plays no part in consciousness
Because consciousness needs the brainstem activating system and both hemispheres, so one hemisphere's loss leaves the system working
Because hemispheric lesions only affect movement
Because coma always comes from the medulla
quiz.explanation: Wakefulness depends on the interaction between the reticular activating system in the brainstem tegmentum and the cerebral hemispheres. Losing one hemisphere leaves the brainstem system and the other hemisphere working, so the child is impaired but awake. The cortex does take part in consciousness, which is why bilateral hemispheric dysfunction causes coma. Hemispheric lesions affect language, attention, vision and sensation as well as movement. The activating system lies in the pons and midbrain, while the medulla is concerned with breathing and circulation.

quiz.question: A resident writes "patient obtunded" in a sedated child's notes. Why does the attending ask for a rewrite?
options: Because obtunded is the wrong grade; the child is stuporous
Because sedated children cannot be assessed
Because labels such as obtunded mean different things to different readers; describing the stimulus and the response lets the next examiner tell whether the child has changed
Because only the coma scale score should be written
quiz.explanation: Brazis recommends describing responsiveness in plain words, recording the stimulus used, what the child did and how long the response lasted. Labels such as obtunded or stuporous are applied inconsistently, so they cannot show a change between examinations, and showing change is the purpose of serial assessment. Swapping one label for another simply repeats the problem. Sedated children can and must be assessed, with the sedation recorded alongside the findings. A coma scale score is useful, but it compresses away details that matter for localization, such as which side moves.

quiz.question: A 10-year-old has two weeks of morning headaches and vomiting. She cannot look up, her eyes rest slightly downward, and she has a mild left sixth-nerve palsy. Which finding best tells you where the lesion is?
options: The failure of upgaze, which points to pressure on the posterior commissure in the pineal region
The left sixth-nerve palsy, which places the lesion in the left pons
Neither, because once the pressure is raised every eye sign is a false localizing sign
The vomiting, which places the lesion in the medulla
quiz.explanation: A tumor pressing on the posterior commissure, such as a pineal tumor, disturbs vertical gaze and can hold the eyes tonically down (Pearl 2014, p. 40), so the failure of upgaze is a true address. The sixth-nerve palsy is tempting because it is lateralized, but the sixth nerve is an early casualty of raised pressure from any cause and is the commonest false localizing sign (Pearl 2014, p. 43; Brazis 2011, p. 622). Declaring every eye sign false throws away the one that does localize. Morning vomiting here fits raised pressure better than a medullary lesion.

signOff: The resident examines a child with depressed consciousness, describes responsiveness in plain words, and states the level of the lesion or that the process is diffuse, with a faculty reader.

opener.parable: Sometimes the examination refuses to settle on a single level. The pupils point one way, the breathing another and the eye movements somewhere else again. That disagreement is useful in its own right, because it usually means something is affecting the whole brain at once.
opener.history: The warning triad of rising intracranial pressure (a slowing pulse, a widening pulse pressure and a change in breathing) carries the name of Harvey Cushing.
